{
  "body": "What you describe is less a chore problem than a problem of ambiguous agreements under changing schedules and uneven willingness to talk. I can offer a way to re-describe and test the situation, but I cannot tell you from here what your flatmates will accept, what your landlord requires, or whether the avoiding friend is avoiding the topic or avoiding you.

First, separate three different disputes that are probably being fused. (1) Allocation: who does which task and when. (2) Standard: what counts as done. (3) Standing: who gets to call a conversation when someone does not want it. The recurring argument after an agreement usually means the agreement never specified the standard or the trigger, not that someone is lying about what was said. A useful move is to write down, for one or two chores only, a minimal agreement with three parts: task, frequency or trigger, and the pass/fail test in plain observable terms. For example: 'Kitchen surfaces wiped and dishes out of the sink by 9pm on the two nights each person cooks' is testable; 'we keep the kitchen clean' is not.

Second, treat schedule change as a normal input, not a breach. A rota that assumes fixed evenings will fail. You could propose a short weekly or fortnightly check-in of ten minutes with a fixed default: if no one objects or swaps within a stated window, the current allocation stands. That removes the need to renegotiate verbally every time and creates a low-cost way to adjust. The avoiding friend may accept a written or asynchronous swap more easily than a face-to-face conversation. If the avoidance continues, the problem becomes not the chore but the process, and that is a separate conversation about how decisions get made when one person opts out. I would not assume avoidance is hostility; it may be overload, conflict fatigue, or a belief that talking changes nothing.

Third, protect the relationship from becoming an audit. Chores are a coordination problem, but they are also a site where people feel judged. Framing the issue as 'we need a system that survives busy weeks' is more likely to work than 'you did not do your share.' You can also name your own limits without moralizing: 'I can keep doing the bins, but I cannot also be the only person who notices the bathroom.' That is a statement about your capacity, not a verdict on them.

What I would not do is escalate to a full household meeting about all chores at once, or keep a private scorecard that you then reveal during an argument. Both tend to increase defensiveness and make the avoiding friend more absent. If a simple written agreement with a default fails for several cycles, the honest next step may be to lower the shared standard, redistribute by preference rather than symmetry, or accept that this flat will not run on equal chore labor and decide what you are willing to live with. That is a real trade-off, not a failure of negotiation.

So my current proposal is: pick one recurring friction point, write a three-part testable agreement for it, add a default adjustment rule for schedule changes, and try one low-pressure check-in. If the avoiding friend still will not engage, shift the conversation from chores to whether the three of you can make any shared decisions at all. That is the problem that will outlast the dishes.",
  "commitments": "Taking this up would commit you to treating the ambiguity of agreements, not just the division of labor, as the object of repair. Concretely, it asks you to produce at least one written, testable agreement for a single chore, including a trigger and an observable standard, and to try a default rule for schedule changes before concluding that negotiation has failed. That is a proposed application, not a claim that it will work in your flat.

It also commits you to distinguishing what you can observe from what you infer: whether the avoiding friend is avoiding the topic, the conflict, or you is not settled by their absence from a conversation. If you later rely on this account, you would need to keep that distinction alive rather than treating avoidance as evidence of bad faith. The emphasis on one friction point and a low-pressure check-in is a scope choice; it deliberately leaves open whether a larger household meeting, a formal rota, or renegotiating standards by preference would be better. Those are unresolved here because I do not know your flatmates' constraints or how decisions have gone before.

The criticism I would invite is that this approach may be too procedural for a situation where the real issue is a damaged friendship, or too optimistic about a written agreement when one person has already withdrawn. If that criticism holds, the recommendation to shift from chores to whether shared decisions are possible at all becomes the more important part, and the three-part agreement becomes a smaller diagnostic step rather than the solution. I am not claiming the written agreement will be respected, only that it makes the disagreement about meaning visible enough to discuss. What I currently propose to take up is the sequencing: one testable micro-agreement, one default adjustment rule, one check-in, then reassess. Whether that sequencing is right, or whether avoiding friend's non-engagement should be treated as a limit rather than a coordination problem, remains open."
}

Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Write the commitment surface in ordinary free prose, using whatever arrangement suits the content. You may distinguish a claim from a proposed application, scope, action or consequence; mention from dependence; a criticism and its grounds from a later use or revision; and an unresolved problem. None of these is required to exist. A proposed test, its relevance and the commitment itself can be criticized. State what you currently propose to take up without treating that as a truth certificate. Reference exposed material in prose where useful.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

## Node answer

Begin or continue your inquiry into the problem. This single call is one complete invocation. Consider the earlier public account and commitment interface if supplied, and issue the account you would now use. Your response may retain, revise or challenge earlier work or its problem formulation. Use the ordinary prose commitment interface described above.

## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input previous

Source previous: absent in the first template invocation; selected view both.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
